turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Fourie. Shame, long wait hey. Shoes off, on the scale before Dr Naidoo sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sorry sister. The robot by the garage was out and a bakkie just sat there. I don't know, we were stuck ages.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I told her to leave earlier. I stay with her, so I came along. Ag, we're here.

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Weight is fifty-four, ag sorry, I misread it, fifty-two kilograms. Last time in March you were sixty-eight. Your last pressure was one-forty, and today it's one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse eighty-four, temperature thirty-eight point three degrees.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty-eight? Eish. I don't know, sister. My clothes feel the same to me.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. He's free now. Sharp, in you go, I'll leave the chart.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Howzit. Dr Naidoo. Sit, please. What can I do for you today?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this pain, doctor, up on the right of my stomach, under the ribs. Quite bad, it comes on after fatty food and then it lasts for hours. The antacid takes the edge off a bit, not all the way.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about an episode, from the start, what sets it...
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. It comes after fatty food. Vetkoek, boerewors, the fried chicken. Then it sits there for...
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): For hours. She holds her side half the night.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Hours. Sometimes the whole evening. I don't know the number.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): And when did it all begin?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): About three weeks. Since the braai at Uncle Piet's. She was alright before that.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, no, Lindi, it was longer than that braai. I don't know, doctor, maybe two months? I can't say the day, I really don't know.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Somewhere between three weeks and two months, then, and nobody can give me the date. We'll leave it. Do you vomit when it comes?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Once. That night I brought everything up. Not again since.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the vomit?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. There was no blood.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yellow eyes, or a yellow colour in the skin?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I looked in the mirror. Not yellow.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it travel to the shoulder, or through to your back?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She said it goes...
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, let me. Not the shoulder. The back I don't know, doctor. I sit all day doing admin at the primary school, so maybe I'm just stiff.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, and my breathing is fine.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the waterworks?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No trouble there. That's fine.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dark urine, pale stools, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I don't look. Sorry.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then I won't write it. Have you had any operations?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never had surgery.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Our mother had her gallbladder out, though. She always said the pain was like this.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Mom had the gallbladder surgery, in Durban. I don't know which year.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Useful. And medicines, what do you take?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Only that antacid liquid from the chemist. Gaviskon, I call it. I don't know, doctor, maybe ten mils when the pain comes. It takes the edge off, not completely.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Gaviscon, you mean. You drink it when the pain comes. Is ten mils definite?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Maybe ten mils. The little cup confuses me. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the dose is uncertain, we'll say maybe ten mils and not dress it up. Anything else, even a supermarket tablet?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just that.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or food? Swelling, rash?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't have any.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Onto the bed for me, knees a little bent. I'm going to press under the right ribs.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Ow. That's it, right there. Not the left.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tender in the right upper abdomen, and it catches when you breathe in. The rest is soft, no guarding. Your eyes aren't yellow, and there's no rash on the skin.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So maybe it's just indigestion? I don't know, doctor. I was hoping for something small.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll think out loud. Pain for hours under the right ribs after fatty meals, you vomited once, your mother had the gallbladder removed, and you're sitting at thirty-eight point three. Most likely biliary colic, a stone irritating the gallbladder. I can't lock that in without tests.

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): The Gaviscon helping a little keeps a gastritis on the list, though I think it's less likely. Fatty meals pull me toward the gallbladder, not the stomach. Tests will have to decide.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm booking blood tests today, liver functions and a full blood count, and an abdominal ultrasound, the sonar, for the gallbladder. The sonar will be booked within the week. These are arranged, not a wait-and-see.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods today? I have to fetch my boy from soccer at four. I don't know if I make it.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Lab's just down the passage, Mrs Fourie. I'll take you straight after, it isn't long. Sonar is a different day.

[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cut the fatty meals for now, the vetkoek and boerewors and fried chicken, and keep the Gaviscon when it bites. Come back in two weeks for the results, whether you feel better or not. If the pain gets savage, or you can't stop vomiting, or you turn yellow, go to casualty and don't wait for that visit.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Two weeks. If the sonar is normal, then what? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then we rethink, simple as that. And Lindi, before you ask, no operation talk today just because mom had one. Far too early. Sister, she's ready for the bloods.

spec.situation: Woman with right-upper stomach pain after fatty meals, lasting hours, once with vomiting; takes antacid; mother had gallbladder surgery; blood tests and ultrasound planned.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Family member said they stay with her; no sister mentioned.

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty; duration is uncertain/disputed, not certain.

bad.reason: Current Gaviscon use supported, but dose is uncertain 'maybe ten mils,' not definite 10 ml.

bad.text: The sister said the pain had been present for about three weeks and the patient said maybe two months, and they did not agree an exact duration. (type=duration_disagreement, related_entities=symptoms[0], resolution_status=partially_resolved)

omissions.text: Negative finding not recorded: patient denied back radiation only as uncertain ('The back I don't know'), so back radiation should not be assumed absent.
Negative finding not recorded: patient did not know whether urine was dark or stools were pale, so these features were asked but remain unknown.
Physical examination omission: abdomen was otherwise soft.
Follow-up instruction detail not recorded: return in two weeks for results whether she feels better or not.

Investigation/logistics detail not recorded: abdominal ultrasound/sonar is arranged rather than wait-and-see, and bloods are to be done straight away with the nurse taking her to the lab; sonar is on a different day.
Weight-loss context not recorded: nurse stated prior weight in March was 68 kg compared with current 52 kg.
Medication recorded too definitively: Gaviscon dose was uncertain ('maybe 10 mL', measuring cup confuses her), not a definite 10 mL.
